newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Apartheid era killer says general gave the orders.
newsitem.headline: Apartheid era killer says general gave the orders.

text.p: A convicted apartheid era assassin took the stand on Monday in a South African court and described how a former superior ordered him to execute black guerrillas.

Eugene de Kock, found guilty last month of six murders and scores of lesser crimes committed while he led a notorious death-squad unit, told the packed Pretoria Supreme Court that the brutality of guerrilla warfare turned him into a hardened killer.
He was referring to executions of his counter-insurgency comrades who fought guerrillas in neighbouring Rhodesia (now Zimbabwe) in the early 1970s.
"It made me decide: you shoot first and ask questions later," de Kock, 47, said.

Cabinet ministers from President Nelson Mandela's African National Congress were among those crammed into the court where de Kock took the stand for the first time in his trial to try to persuade the judge to pass a lenient sentence.

De Kock, who said he was apartheid's most effective assassin, has also applied to Archbishop Desmond Tutu's "truth commission" for amnesty. Getting it would depend partly on his telling all -- something de Kock reportedly pledged to do.

Safety and Security Minister Sydney Mufamadi and Deputy National Intelligence Minister Joe Nhlanhla were present in court as de Kock described how a little-known General Dreyer had ordered him to execute three black guerrillas in South-West Africa (now Namibia) where de Kock also served in a counter-insurgency unit in the 1970s.
Anti-apartheid activists are hoping de Kock will implicate better known senior officials who served in former president F.W. de Klerk's last white government.
The only official to be charged so far is former defence minister Magnus Malan, whose trial for alleged complicity in a 1987 massacre of 13 men, women and children is nearing its end.
Lawyers defending de Kock during his 18-month trial have said he is suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder and that they may cite this as a mitigating factor.
The career policeman, arrested shortly after the all-race elections in 1994 buried apartheid, was raised in a strict religious and nationalistic home.
But he denied having been a racist and said he was annoyed by the double standards he witnessed in the South African forces during the wars in Rhodesia and South-West Africa.
He said whenever he called from the field for help for a wounded operative, radio control would ask if he was black or white.
"(Only) if they were white, they would send the helicopters very quickly. That sort of thing was unacceptable to me," he said.
